Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
Three months ago, Julian stood in the crowded downtown transit station when a man in a gray coat lunged toward his younger brother, Marcus. It happened in a fraction of a second. Julian’s eyes locked onto Marcus’s forearms, the way they were suddenly bruised and splayed against the tiled floor, the sharp, copper-and-rain scent filling Julian’s throat. He tried to speak, to call out, but the memory would not form into sentences. Instead, his mind simply held the scene: a crisp, unblinking photograph of his brother’s wrists pinned against the ground, the angle of the elbow, the dark stain spreading across the concrete. In the weeks that followed, Julian found his body refusing to listen to logic. Every sudden movement in the street—a cyclist swerving, a door slamming—sparked an immediate, rigid guard in his shoulders. His chest tightened as if the danger were still pressing down on him, even though the transit station was now just a quiet platform. He began to notice the photograph images again, not as memories but as overlays on his present: the way a barista’s hands gripped a cup, the shape of a passerby’s collarbone, the specific curve of a stranger’s forearm. When his wife, Clara, mentioned her sister’s recent hospital visit or made a passing remark about family safety, Julian’s jaw would lock. He could not explain why the words felt like alarms; he simply knew they did. Julian stopped watching television altogether. News segments, crime dramas, even documentaries about accidents were impossible to sit through. The images and sounds in those programs felt too close to the stillness of the transit station, so he would turn toward the door before the first scene began. He also stopped staying in one room for more than a few minutes. If he found himself alone in their apartment’s bedroom, the quiet would press against his ribs until he had to step into the living room or walk the streets. He began to carry a small pocketknife, not to use it, but to dig the blade into his thumb when the pressure in his chest became too heavy. The physical sting was the only thing that seemed to cut through the static, even though he hated that it worked. His unemployment had become a daily reality, but it was no longer just an empty calendar. Julian had spent years in the city’s public works department, coordinating logistics and walking site inspections. Now, the idea of navigating a crowded street or reading a complex schedule made his hands tremble. He could not rely on himself to make a decision without his mind fracturing into those same frozen photographs. He had come to believe that his body was working against him, firing off emergency signals in a world that had not changed, and that he was no longer capable of the steady, deliberate work that had once defined him. He stopped applying for other jobs. The apartment, which used to be filled with blueprints and coffee cups, now felt like a place where he had to keep moving just to breathe. Clara’s attempts to talk about her family’s health felt like pulling at a live wire, and they had stopped planning meals together for fear of the crowded restaurants. Sleep became a series of broken fragments. He would lie down, close his eyes, and then feel or act as if the gray coat were lunging again, his body jerking awake before he could realize he was in his own bed. When he did sleep, it was shallow, broken by the same sharp smells and the same impossible stillness. It was the nights that finally pushed him to schedule an appointment with a clinic. He had reached a point where the constant vigilance, the isolation he forced upon himself, and the recurring physical relief he sought were draining him completely. He hoped to find a way to quiet the alarms in his nervous system, to sleep through the night, and to stop watching every stranger’s hands. What frightened him most was that he might never trust himself to be still again, or that he would lose Clara to the weight of a life he could no longer share. He wanted, above all, to stop running from a moment that refused to stay in the past.
